title: Understanding genetic carrier screening: Q&A with Dr. Leslie Saltzman
summary: Learn what genetic carrier screening is, how it works, who should consider it, and how results can help guide pregnancy and fertility choices.
body_markdown:
Many people have heard of genetic testing, but fewer are familiar with carrier screening, a type of genetic testing that can help individuals and couples prepare for pregnancy. For some, genetic testing can feel confusing or even overwhelming. The good news is that carrier screening can provide insight into reproductive risks and help individuals make informed decisions for their future.


To help answer common questions, we spoke with Dr. Leslie Saltzman, vice president and medical discipline director for consumer health at Labcorp, who shares what patients should know about carrier screening before or during pregnancy. Dr. Saltzman is a board-certified internal medicine physician with extensive experience in women’s health.


## What is genetic carrier screening?


Carrier screening is a genetic test that looks for certain gene changes linked to inherited health conditions. A person who carries one or more of these gene changes is called a carrier.


“Genetic carrier screening is a type of genetic test that looks at your DNA to see whether you carry changes in certain genes that could be passed on to your children,” says Dr. Saltzman. “Most carriers are healthy and don’t have any symptoms, so testing can provide information that wouldn’t otherwise be known.”


In fact, it's estimated that[everyone carries three to five genetic variants](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3484657/) that could be passed on to their children. Carrier screening helps identify whether you carry variants associated with specific inherited disorders.


## Why do doctors recommend genetic carrier screening?


Carrier screening can provide valuable information to support individuals and families as they plan for or navigate pregnancy.


"Carrier screening gives people more information before or early in pregnancy, when they have the most options available to them," says Dr. Saltzman.


Testing can help you:


- Understand your chances of having a child with certain inherited conditions
- Make informed family-planning decisions
- Learn about available testing or treatment options
- Prepare for specialized care and resources if needed


"For some conditions, treatment has to be administered soon (or immediately) after birth for it to be effective," Dr. Saltzman adds.


## Who should consider genetic carrier screening?


[Current medical guidelines](https://www.acog.org/clinical/clinical-guidance/committee-opinion/articles/2017/03/carrier-screening-for-genetic-conditions) recommend offering carrier screening to anyone who is planning a pregnancy or is already pregnant.


“People are often surprised to learn they are carriers because being a carrier typically doesn’t affect your own health,” says Dr. Saltzman. “Most carriers feel completely healthy and have no symptoms, which is why genetic carrier screening can uncover information that wouldn’t otherwise be apparent.”


Most carriers also have no known family history of the condition they carry. Because inherited conditions can affect people from all backgrounds, carrier screening may be helpful regardless of ethnicity, ancestry, or family history.


## What genetic conditions can carrier screening detect?


The answer depends on the type and size of the screening panel you and your healthcare provider choose.


Many carrier screening panels include conditions such as:


- Cystic fibrosis
- Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA)
- Sickle cell disease, thalassemia, and other hemoglobin disorders


Some expanded carrier screening panels can screen for hundreds of inherited conditions.


"Your healthcare provider can help you choose the screening panel that best fits your needs," says Dr. Saltzman.


## How does genetic carrier screening work?


Carrier screening is a simple process with speedy results. Most people can complete testing during a routine healthcare visit.


"It usually requires only a blood sample or saliva sample," she says. "There's no special preparation needed."


The sample is sent to a laboratory, where it is analyzed for genetic changes associated with specific inherited conditions. Within approximately two to three weeks, your healthcare provider will review the results with you and discuss any next steps, if needed.


## What does it mean to be a carrier of a genetic condition?


Finding out you're a carrier does not mean you have a disease.


"I always remind patients to take a deep breath," says Dr. Saltzman. "Being a carrier is common and usually has no impact on your health."


What matters is whether your reproductive partner is also a carrier of the same condition. Many inherited disorders follow an autosomal recessive pattern, meaning a child would need to inherit a gene change from both parents to be affected.


## What happens if both partners are carriers for the same genetic condition?


If both partners carry the same recessive condition, each pregnancy has a 25% chance of resulting in a child with that condition.


While that information can feel stressful, there are resources available to help.


"One of the first steps is meeting with a[genetic counselor](https://www.labcorp.com/education-events/articles/ask-expert-what-you-need-know-about-working-genetic-counselor) ," says Dr. Saltzman. "They can explain your results, answer questions, and discuss options in a way that's personalized for your family."


Depending on your situation, discussions may include:


- Additional testing during pregnancy
- IVF with preimplantation genetic testing
- Using donor eggs or donor sperm
- Planning for specialized care after birth


"There is no one-size-fits-all decision," she adds. "The goal is to give families information and support."


## Does insurance cover genetic carrier screening?


Insurance coverage varies by plan, but carrier screening is often covered when recommended as part of preconception or prenatal care.


"I encourage patients to check directly with their insurance provider to understand their benefits and potential out-of-pocket costs," says Dr. Saltzman.


Many laboratories offer programs to help patients understand the cost of testing and explore financial assistance options when available. According to Labcorp internal billing data, many insured patients pay no out-of-pocket for carrier screening.


## How do I choose the right genetic carrier screening test?


There isn't one test that's right for everyone.


"The best test depends on your personal history, family history, and how much information you want from the screening," explains Dr. Saltzman.


Your healthcare provider can help determine whether a targeted panel or a broader expanded panel makes the most sense for you.


“Some people may benefit from a targeted panel that screens for specific genetic conditions based on their family history or ancestry,” says Dr. Saltzman. “Others may prefer an expanded carrier screening panel, which evaluates a broader range of inherited conditions, including many that may not be linked to a known family history.”


## When is the best time to get genetic carrier screening? ****


Before pregnancy is ideal, says Dr. Saltzman.


"Screening before conception gives patients the most time to understand their results and consider their options," she explains.


However, carrier screening can still provide valuable information during pregnancy.


"If you didn't have testing before becoming pregnant, it's absolutely still worth discussing with your healthcare provider."


## I had genetic carrier screening before my first pregnancy. Do I need it again?


Often, no. "Your carrier status doesn't change over time," says Dr. Saltzman.


However, it may be worth discussing additional screening with your healthcare provider if:


- You have a new reproductive partner
- Your previous screening was limited


Your healthcare provider can review your past testing and help determine whether updated screening may be beneficial.


## What if I feel overwhelmed by genetic testing?


It is completely normal to feel nervous when you first hear about genetic testing, says Dr. Saltzman. “Remember that carrier screening is optional, and support is available every step of the way.”


She encourages patients to talk openly with their healthcare provider and consider[speaking with a genetic counselor](https://womenshealth.labcorp.com/patients/services/genetic-counseling) if they have concerns.


"The purpose of carrier screening isn't to create fear," says Dr. Saltzman. "It's to provide information that can help you better understand your options and prepare for the future in a way that feels right for you and your family."


## What to remember about genetic carrier screening


Carrier screening is a test that can help you understand your chances of having a child with an inherited disorder. While testing is optional, many people choose it because the information can help them prepare and plan for the future. If you have questions or concerns, talk with your healthcare provider or a genetic counselor. They can help you understand your options and provide support every step of the way.
